card.core: Peace comes from training the ruling part to act with reason and justice, seeing all else as natural and fleeting.

lessons.lesson: You will meet difficult people; understanding their ignorance prevents anger.
lessons.why: They act wrongly from ignorance of good and evil, so you can pity rather than hate them, remembering you share the same intelligence.

lessons.lesson: Judge each act as if it were your last, with dignity and justice.
lessons.why: This strips away carelessness, hypocrisy, self-love, and discontent; few things are needed for a quiet life.

lessons.lesson: Desires cause more blame than anger because they are voluntary.
lessons.why: Theophrastus says anger comes with pain and involuntary contraction, while desire is chosen from pleasure and is more intemperate.

card.remember: The present is all you can lose; the past and future you do not have.

terms.meaning: The mind or reason, the core self that can choose its responses.
The inner guiding spirit or reason, which must be kept pure from passion and thoughtlessness.

diagram.why: The chapter presents a series of ethical reflections without a clear causal or sequential structure.

card.core: Read the best books deliberately in their original languages, for true reading is a heroic exercise that most never attempt.

lessons.lesson: Written language is a separate, higher tongue than speech.
lessons.why: The chapter distinguishes the mother tongue learned unconsciously from the father tongue, a reserved written expression that must be learned deliberately.

lessons.lesson: Translations cannot substitute for reading classics in the original.
lessons.why: The chapter claims Homer has never been printed in English and that cheap translations leave the ancients as solitary and remote as ever.

lessons.lesson: Easy reading stultifies the intellect and wastes life.
lessons.why: The chapter describes novel readers as machines with dulled sight and stagnant faculties, comparing such books to gingerbread baked daily.

card.remember: Books must be read as deliberately and reservedly as they were written.

terms.meaning: The noblest recorded thoughts of man, the only oracles which are not decayed.
Written language, a reserved and select expression too significant to be heard by the ear.
Great works that remain in a language dead to degenerate times, requiring labor to understand.
Reading true books in a true spirit, a noble intellectual exercise that tasks the reader more than any customary exercise.

diagram.title: How do true reading and easy reading differ?

rows.a: Steady intention of a whole life

card.core: A prince must avoid being hated or despised, for these breed conspiracies, and popular goodwill is his best shield.

lessons.lesson: Seizing property or women makes a prince hated above all.
lessons.why: When neither property nor honor is touched, most men live content; only the ambition of a few remains, easily curbed.

lessons.lesson: Showing fickleness, frivolity, or irresolution makes a prince contemptible.
lessons.why: He must instead display greatness, courage, gravity, and fortitude, and make his judgments irrevocable so no one can deceive or bypass him.

lessons.lesson: Hatred and contempt doom a prince; goodwill protects him.
lessons.why: Roman emperors like Pertinax, Alexander, and Maximinus fell to conspiracy from these; Marcus, esteemed by both orders, lived honored.

card.remember: Hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones.

terms.meaning: Held in contempt for being fickle, frivolous, effeminate, mean-spirited, or irresolute.
Made an object of loathing by rapacity, violating property or women, or cruelty.
A secret plot by subjects to overthrow or kill the prince.
The people's esteem and affection for the prince, which makes conspirators fear offending them.

diagram.title: How does hatred or contempt lead to ruin?

card.core: Society may coerce an individual only to prevent harm to others, never for his own good.

lessons.lesson: Self-government is a fiction; the majority rules the rest.
lessons.why: The 'people' wielding power are not the same as those it is exercised over, and the majority may oppress a minority.

lessons.lesson: Social tyranny goes deeper than political oppression.
lessons.why: It works through opinion rather than law, leaves fewer means of escape, penetrates the details of life, and enslaves the soul.

lessons.lesson: Rules of conduct rest on custom and class interest, not reason.
lessons.why: People follow their own liking, class feelings and servility to masters, and never suspect any difficulty in their standards.

card.remember: Ask of any interference: does this conduct harm anyone besides the actor?

terms.meaning: The nature and limits of the power society may legitimately exercise over the individual.
The majority imposing its opinions and practices on dissenters, by law or by opinion.
Conduct that affects only the agent himself, or others only with their free consent.
Evil or injury done to someone else; the only warrant for compulsion.

card.core: When the Quaker Assembly would not fund defense, Franklin raised an army of volunteers by pamphlet, lottery and persuasion.

lessons.lesson: A pamphlet can move more people than a law.
lessons.why: Plain Truth was written and read aloud; twelve hundred signed at once and the total grew past ten thousand.

lessons.lesson: Quaker objection came from principle, not numbers.
lessons.why: At the fire company vote, only one of twenty-two Quakers opposed; others stayed away or offered votes quietly.

lessons.lesson: Printed creeds trap a sect that learns.
lessons.why: The Dunker founder refused to print his faith, fearing members would feel bound and stop improving.

card.remember: Never ask, never refuse, nor ever resign an office.

terms.meaning: A volunteer army raised by citizens signing a paper, not by law.
The Penn family, who owned and governed Pennsylvania.
Franklin's joke for gunpowder, since the Assembly funded bread but not powder.

card.core: Species and varieties cannot be cleanly separated; they are stages on one continuous series, and that supports common descent.

lessons.lesson: Varieties are incipient species, not a separate kind of thing.
lessons.why: Individual differences blend into slight varieties, then marked varieties, subspecies and species by an insensible series; Darwin calls a well-marked variety an incipient species.

lessons.lesson: Dominant, wide-ranging species of large genera produce the most varieties.
lessons.why: Tables of plants from twelve countries and beetles from two districts show species of larger genera yield more varieties; being already dominant, their offspring inherit the advantages.

lessons.lesson: Species of large genera resemble varieties in being closely and unequally allied, with restricted ranges.
lessons.why: They differ by unusually small amounts and cluster like satellites round other species; Watson found doubtful species average 6.9 provinces against 7.7 for varieties and 14.3 for their parent species.

card.remember: Where many large trees grow, we expect to find saplings.

terms.meaning: In this book, an arbitrarily given label for a set of closely resembling individuals, for convenience, differing only in degree from variety.
A less distinct, more fluctuating form; in Darwin's view an incipient species, a species in the making.
The slight differences among offspring of the same parents, or among individuals of one species in one locality.
A species more numerous in individuals and more widely diffused than its close competitors of the same group.
A considerable deviation of structure, generally injurious or not useful to the species, grading into varieties.

diagram.title: How a difference becomes a species

card.core: Raskolnikov abandons his plan as impossible, then a chance overheard remark makes it certain.

lessons.lesson: He confesses he could never swing the axe
lessons.why: Waking from the horse dream, he says flatly he would never bring himself to it, yet goes on torturing himself with the thought

lessons.lesson: Relief is a feeling, not a decision
lessons.why: He prays to be shown his path and renounces the dream, but only the feeling changes; the reasoning stays untouched

lessons.lesson: Chance information removes the last obstacle
lessons.why: He overhears that Lizaveta will be out at seven, so the old woman will be alone, exactly what his plan needed

card.remember: The abscess in his heart bursts and he feels free, yet freedom only clears ground for the plan.

terms.meaning: Raskolnikov's word for his earlier visit to the pawnbroker, a trial run of the plan rather than an errand

card.core: A healthy, fortunate man discovers life has no meaning, and the truth drives him toward suicide.

lessons.lesson: Knowing the truth is what makes life unlivable.
lessons.why: Once sober, he sees that death will erase everything he does; while intoxicated with life he could live, but he cannot return to that.

lessons.lesson: He distrusts himself around his own death.
lessons.why: He hides a cord and stops going out shooting, not because he wants to die but because the pull is so quick and seductive.

lessons.lesson: Family and art lose their sweetness once the truth is seen.
lessons.why: Both were honey drops distracting him from the dragon; art he now calls a fraud, since it adorns a life he no longer wants.

card.remember: The fable is not a fable: the dragon is real and the honey no longer tastes sweet.

terms.meaning: The state of living on borrowed meaning, absorbed in habits and hopes, without noticing that death cancels everything.
Any pleasure, in the fable and in his life: family love, art, success. It distracts from the dragon but does not remove it.

diagram.title: Why he cannot escape his torment
